cards.front: What is the definition of cumulative frequency?
cards.back: The running total of the frequencies.

options.text: The running total of the frequencies.
options.explanation: Cumulative frequency is found by successively adding each frequency to the total from the preceding classes, producing a running total through the data set.
Subtracting consecutive frequencies compares individual classes rather than accumulating them. Cumulative frequency is the running total obtained by adding frequencies successively.

options.text: The average of all the frequencies.
options.explanation: Calculating a mean would give an average class frequency, not an accumulated count. Cumulative frequency is the running total of the frequencies.

options.text: The highest of the individual frequencies.
options.explanation: Selecting the largest frequency identifies the modal class rather than the accumulated total. Cumulative frequency is the running total of all frequencies reached so far.

cards.front: The final value in a cumulative frequency table must equal the [ ___ ].
cards.back: The final value in a cumulative frequency table must equal the total frequency.

options.explanation: The last cumulative frequency includes every observation in every class, so it must equal the total frequency of the complete data set.
Class width is the difference between a class’s boundaries and is unrelated to the final accumulated count. The final cumulative frequency equals the total frequency.
The upper boundary is an endpoint on the horizontal axis, not a number of observations. The final cumulative frequency must equal the total frequency.
Frequency density is calculated by dividing frequency by class width, so it is not the final accumulated count. The last cumulative frequency equals the total frequency.

cards.front: When plotting a cumulative frequency graph, which value from the class interval is used for the horizontal coordinate?
cards.back: The upper boundary (upper bound).

options.explanation: Each cumulative total counts observations up to the end of its class interval, so it is plotted against that class’s upper boundary.
The cumulative total for a class includes values throughout that class, not merely values below its lower boundary. Each total is plotted at the upper boundary.
Midpoints are commonly used for frequency polygons, which makes this a tempting confusion. Cumulative frequencies are plotted against the upper class boundaries.
Class width measures the size of an interval rather than locating its endpoint. A cumulative frequency point uses the class’s upper boundary as its horizontal coordinate.

cards.front: What is the starting coordinate for a cumulative frequency graph?
cards.back: The lower boundary of the first class at cumulative frequency 0.

options.text: The lower boundary of the first class at cumulative frequency 0.
options.explanation: Before the first class begins, no observations have yet been accumulated. The graph therefore starts at the first lower boundary with cumulative frequency zero.

options.text: The upper boundary of the first class at cumulative frequency 0.
options.explanation: By the first upper boundary, all observations in the first class have been counted, so the cumulative frequency is not zero. Start at the first lower boundary.

options.text: The lower boundary of the first class at cumulative frequency 1.
options.explanation: This off-by-one error assumes counting starts with one observation. Before the first class begins, none have been counted, so the starting cumulative frequency is zero.

options.text: The midpoint of the first class at cumulative frequency 0.
options.explanation: The midpoint lies inside the first class, where values may already have accumulated. The graph starts at the first class’s lower boundary with cumulative frequency zero.

cards.front: A common mistake is plotting the [ ___ ] instead of the upper boundary.
cards.back: A common mistake is plotting the midpoint instead of the upper boundary.

options.explanation: Midpoints are used when plotting frequency polygons, but cumulative frequency points must use upper class boundaries. Confusing the two graph types is a common error.
Although lower boundaries are relevant to class intervals, the commonly highlighted plotting error is using the midpoint. Cumulative totals should be plotted at upper boundaries.
Class width describes the size of an interval and is not normally used as a plotted horizontal coordinate. The common error is plotting the midpoint instead of the upper boundary.
Frequency density is a vertical-axis quantity used for histograms, not a horizontal class value. The common mistake is plotting the midpoint rather than the upper boundary.

cards.front: A common mistake is plotting the midpoint instead of the [ ___ ].
cards.back: A common mistake is plotting the midpoint instead of the upper boundary.

options.explanation: A cumulative total represents the number of observations up to the end of a class, so each point belongs at that class’s upper boundary.
Using the lower boundary places the cumulative total at the beginning of the class, before that class has been counted. It belongs at the upper boundary.
Class width measures the span of an interval rather than its horizontal endpoint. Cumulative frequency points are plotted using each class’s upper boundary.
A lower limit marks the beginning of a stated class and does not show where its cumulative total is reached. The required value is the upper boundary.

cards.front: Individual points on a cumulative frequency graph should be joined with a [ ___ ].
cards.back: Individual points on a cumulative frequency graph should be joined with a smooth increasing curve.

options.explanation: Cumulative frequency cannot decrease as more observations are included. A smooth increasing curve represents the growing running total and allows estimates of quartiles and percentiles.
Joining every point with rigid straight sections treats the estimated distribution as changing abruptly. At GCSE, cumulative frequency points should be joined by a smooth increasing curve.
A decreasing curve would imply that observations are removed as the measured value increases. Cumulative totals cannot fall, so the curve must increase smoothly.
A frequency polygon joins frequencies plotted at class midpoints and is a different graph type. Cumulative frequency points are joined with a smooth increasing curve.

cards.front: How is the vertical position of the lower quartile ($Q_1$) calculated?
cards.back: $$\frac{N}{4}$ (where $N$ is the total frequency).

options.explanation: The lower quartile marks the point below which one quarter of the observations lie, so its vertical position is calculated as $N \div 4$.
Dividing the total frequency by two locates the median, not the lower quartile. The lower quartile is one quarter of the data, at $\frac{N}{4}$.
Using three quarters of the total locates the upper quartile, $Q_3$. The lower quartile, $Q_1$, is read at cumulative frequency $\frac{N}{4}$.
Dividing by ten locates the first decile rather than the lower quartile. Since a quartile divides the data into four parts, use $\frac{N}{4}$.

cards.front: How is the vertical position of the median calculated?
cards.back: $$\frac{N}{2}$ (where $N$ is the total frequency).

options.explanation: The median divides the ordered data into two equal halves, so it is located at cumulative frequency $\frac{N}{2}$, where $N$ is the total frequency.
Using $\frac{N}{4}$ locates the lower quartile, not the median. The median is halfway through the data, so its vertical position is $\frac{N}{2}$.
Using $\frac{3N}{4}$ locates the upper quartile, not the median. The median splits the data into two equal halves, giving position $\frac{N}{2}$.
Dividing the total frequency by three would locate a third, not the median. The median is halfway through the ordered data, so its position is $\frac{N}{2}$.

cards.front: How is the vertical position of the upper quartile ($Q_3$) calculated?
cards.back: $$\frac{3N}{4}$ (where $N$ is the total frequency).

options.explanation: The upper quartile has 75% of the data at or below it. Therefore, its vertical position is $\frac{3N}{4}$, where $N$ is the total frequency.
Using $\frac{N}{4}$ gives the lower quartile, where 25% of the data lies at or below it. The upper quartile is at $\frac{3N}{4}$.
Using $\frac{N}{2}$ gives the median, which is halfway through the data. The upper quartile is three-quarters through, at $\frac{3N}{4}$.
Reversing the fraction produces a position greater than the total frequency, so it cannot be a quartile. The upper quartile is located at $\frac{3N}{4}$.

cards.front: What are the steps to estimate a quartile from a cumulative frequency graph?
cards.back: Find the position on the vertical axisRead across to the curveRead down to the horizontal axis

options.text: Find the position on the vertical axisRead across to the curveRead down to the horizontal axis
options.explanation: A quartile position is first found using cumulative frequency on the vertical axis. Moving across to the curve and then down gives the corresponding data value.

options.text: Find the position on the horizontal axisRead up to the curveRead across to the vertical axis
options.explanation: This procedure starts with a data value and finds its cumulative frequency, reversing the required process. Begin at the quartile position vertically, then read across and down.

options.text: Find the position on the vertical axisRead down to the curveRead across to the horizontal axis
options.explanation: Reading down from the vertical axis does not lead correctly to the curve. From the quartile position, read horizontally across to the curve and then vertically down.

options.text: Find the position on the horizontal axisRead across to the curveRead up to the vertical axis
options.explanation: Quartile positions are cumulative frequencies, so they must be located on the vertical axis rather than the horizontal axis. Then read across to the curve and down.

cards.front: How is the interquartile range (IQR) calculated?

options.explanation: The interquartile range is the width of the middle 50% of the data. It is calculated by subtracting the lower quartile from the upper quartile.
Adding the quartiles does not measure the distance between them. The interquartile range is the upper quartile minus the lower quartile, so it is $Q_3 - Q_1$.
Reversing the subtraction usually produces a negative value, which cannot represent a spread. Subtract the lower quartile from the upper quartile: $Q_3 - Q_1$.
Subtracting the median $Q_2$ from the upper quartile measures only one section of the box. The full interquartile range is $Q_3 - Q_1$.

cards.front: The interquartile range measures the spread of the [ ___ ] of the data.
cards.back: The interquartile range measures the spread of the middle 50% of the data.

options.explanation: The interval from the lower quartile to the upper quartile contains the central half of the ordered data. Therefore, the interquartile range measures the spread of the middle 50%.
The lowest 50% runs from the minimum to the median, not between the quartiles. The interquartile range measures the spread of the middle 50% of the data.
The quartiles divide the data into four equal 25% sections, and the interval from $Q_1$ to $Q_3$ covers two sections. It therefore contains the middle 50%.
The highest 25% lies above the upper quartile and is not measured by the interquartile range. The IQR covers the middle 50%, from $Q_1$ to $Q_3$.

cards.front: Why are values read from a cumulative frequency graph called estimates?
cards.back: The original data is groupedThe curve is drawn by hand

options.text: The original data is groupedThe curve is drawn by hand
options.explanation: Grouped data does not give every exact individual value, and a hand-drawn curve introduces graphical uncertainty. Consequently, values read from the curve can only be estimates.

options.text: The original data is continuousThe curve is perfectly accurate
options.explanation: Continuous data can be recorded exactly, and a perfectly accurate curve would not itself cause uncertainty. Estimates arise because the data is grouped and the curve is drawn by hand.

options.text: The original data is unorderedThe curve is drawn by computer
options.explanation: Cumulative frequency already organises observations by value, so unordered data is not the issue. Uncertainty comes from grouped intervals and reading from a hand-drawn curve.

options.text: The original data is discreteThe curve is made of straight lines
options.explanation: Discrete data is not automatically estimated, and cumulative frequency curves are not necessarily made of straight lines. The estimates result from grouping and hand-drawing the curve.

cards.front: Which five values are used to construct a box plot?
cards.back: Lowest valueLower quartile ($Q_1$)MedianUpper quartile ($Q_3$)Highest value

options.explanation: A box plot uses the five-number summary: the minimum, lower quartile, median, upper quartile and maximum. These values determine the whisker ends, box edges and central line.
The central line of a standard box plot represents the median, not the mean. The other four values are the minimum, lower quartile, upper quartile and maximum.
The interquartile range determines the box’s width but is not itself one of the five plotted positions. The upper quartile $Q_3$ must be included instead.
The range is a difference, not a plotted endpoint. A box plot needs the actual lowest value alongside the lower quartile, median, upper quartile and highest value.

cards.front: In a box plot, the [ ___ ] line does not have to be in the center of the box.
cards.back: In a box plot, the median line does not have to be in the center of the box.

options.explanation: The line inside the box marks the median. It is centred only when the distances from the median to the lower and upper quartiles are equal.
A standard box plot does not usually display the mean as its internal line. The line marks the median, which need not be centred between the two quartiles.
The range is the numerical difference between the highest and lowest values, not a line inside the box. The internal line represents the median.
Frequency counts how often values occur and is not represented by the line inside a standard box plot. That line shows the median of the data.

cards.front: When comparing two data sets, what does a higher median indicate?
cards.back: The typical value is higher.

options.explanation: The median is the middle value when the data is ordered, so a higher median shows that the typical or central value of the data set is higher.
This reverses the comparison between the medians. A higher median means the middle, or typical, value is higher rather than lower.

options.text: The spread of values is greater.
options.explanation: The median measures central tendency, not spread. A higher median indicates a higher typical value; the IQR or range must be compared to assess spread.
Consistency is determined by measures of spread such as the IQR, not by the median. A higher median only indicates that the typical value is higher.

cards.front: When comparing two data sets, what does a smaller IQR indicate?
cards.back: The data is more consistent (less spread out).

options.text: The data is more consistent (less spread out).
options.explanation: The IQR measures the spread of the middle 50% of the data. A smaller IQR means these values are closer together, indicating greater consistency.

options.text: The data is less consistent (more spread out).
options.explanation: This reverses the meaning of the IQR comparison. A smaller IQR means the middle 50% is less spread out, so the data is more consistent.

options.text: The data has a higher median (larger typical value).
options.explanation: The IQR measures spread and does not determine the median. A smaller IQR indicates more consistent data, but the typical value could be higher or lower.

options.text: The data is more symmetrical (evenly spread out).
options.explanation: The size of the IQR alone does not reveal the distribution’s symmetry. It only shows that the middle 50% is less spread out and therefore more consistent.

cards.front: In the class interval $10 < t \le 20$, what is the upper boundary?

options.explanation: The inequality includes values up to and including 20, so 20 is the upper boundary of the class interval.
The value 10 is the lower boundary, even though it is excluded by the strict inequality. The upper boundary is 20.
Choosing 19 incorrectly treats the data as restricted to whole numbers. The stated class interval extends continuously to 20, which is its upper boundary.
This adds one to the included endpoint, a common whole-number interval mistake. The class ends at 20, so its upper boundary is 20.

cards.front: If the total frequency ($N$) is 80, what is the vertical position for the lower quartile?

options.explanation: The lower quartile is located at one quarter of the total cumulative frequency. With 80 values, its vertical position is $\frac{80}{4}=20$.
Dividing the total frequency by 2 finds the median position, not the lower quartile. The lower quartile is at $\frac{80}{4}=20$.
Using three quarters of the total gives the upper quartile position. The lower quartile uses one quarter, so its vertical position is $\frac{80}{4}=20$.
Dividing by 5 incorrectly splits the data into fifths. Quartiles divide ordered data into four parts, so the lower quartile position is $\frac{80}{4}=20$.

cards.front: How is the range calculated from a box plot?
cards.back: Highest value minus the lowest value.

options.text: Highest value minus the lowest value.
options.explanation: The range measures the full spread of the data, from the minimum to the maximum. It is therefore calculated by subtracting the lowest value from the highest value.

options.text: Highest value plus the lowest value.
options.explanation: Adding the two endpoints does not measure the distance between them. The range is found by subtracting the lowest value from the highest value.

options.text: Upper quartile minus the lower quartile.
options.explanation: Subtracting the lower quartile from the upper quartile calculates the IQR, which measures the middle 50%. The range uses the highest and lowest values instead.

options.text: Lowest value minus the highest value.
options.explanation: This reverses the subtraction and usually produces a negative result. The range is non-negative and is calculated as the highest value minus the lowest value.
